newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Panel proposes floating 100 pct of Israel's El Al.
newsitem.headline: Panel proposes floating 100 pct of Israel's El Al.

text.p: A government panel on Monday recommended that Israel sell its entire holding in El Al Israel Airlines through a public offering in the domestic capital market sometime in 1998.
The proposal marks a new approach to privatising Israel's troubled carrier, which has proven one of the government's toughest sales. El Al is wholly owned by the government.
The panel, headed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's economics adviser Moshe Leon, did not make specific proposals on the ban which stops El Al flying on the Jewish Sabbath and holidays.
The ban on Sabbath flights, imposed at the behest of religious parties, imposes heavy financial costs on El Al.
"Apparently the state will not be able to prevent the company from flying on the Sabbath after it is privatised according to a legal opinion that we have," Leon said.

But Nahum Lagenthal, director-general of the Transport Ministry and a committee member, said they were exploring various options for maintaining what he described as the religious status quo even after El Al is privatised.

He said one option might be to allow El Al to fly on the Sabbath, which runs from sundown Friday and until sundown Saturday, but limit the total number of flights out of Ben-Gurion, Israel's main international airport.
Other airlines would have to reduce their Sabbath flights.
Leon said the committee had opted for a public offering because it would enable the Israeli public to participate and would stimulate the stock market.

The committee proposed that workers be given 10 percent of shares at a 30 percent discount. The government would also establish a special fund to compensate redundant workers before privatising the airline.
The panel also proposed that El Al's security costs, another issue that has dogged the airline's privatisation, be covered by the government on a sliding scale.
The state would finance 90 percent of security costs up to $25 million, two thirds from $25 million to $50 million and half of any costs above that.

The government's last effort to float El Al collapsed after underwriters valued the airline at just $150 million. They assigned the low figure because of the issue of Sabbath flights and security costs.
Newspaper reports said in May said El Al was expecting to post a $40 million loss this year, about half the 1996 loss. The airline declined to comment on the report.
